channel.title: VulnFeed — Security Advisories
channel.description: Aggregated security advisories from GitHub repositories

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Organization list disclosure to customers without organization
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-639, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
A customer user who was not assigned to any organization could have retrieved a list of all organizations in the system via the organization search and autocomplete functions. The list included the names, IDs and active state of organizations the customer had no access to, and in some views also their number of members.
The issue only affected customer accounts without any organization assignment; customers belonging to at least one organization were correctly limited to their own organizations. No ticket content, user details or other organization attributes were exposed, and no data could be modified.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Agents could remove links to objects they had no access to
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Removing a link between two objects only checked the permissions of the requesting agent on one of the linked objects. An agent who was allowed to change a ticket could therefore remove links between that ticket and tickets or knowledge base answers they had no access to, for example tickets in groups they were not a member of. The legacy interface and the GraphQL API were both affected.
No content of the inaccessible object was disclosed, and the agent could not change anything else on it. The impact is limited to the integrity of links: relationships maintained by other teams could be removed without their knowledge. Customers could not exploit this.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Partial administrators could run unintended server components via core workflows
item.description:
CVSS 5.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-470, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Administrators with only the permission to manage core workflows could configure a workflow so that the server ran internal code components that are not meant to be used in core workflows. These components ran whenever the workflow was evaluated, which happens when any user, including customers, opens or changes a form it applies to.
This could have been used to perform actions reserved for other administrative permissions, such as resetting the notification settings of all agents, and to tie up server resources on every form load, slowing down or breaking forms for other users.
Exploitation required an authenticated account with the core workflow administration permission. Installations where only fully trusted users hold this permission were not exposed.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Agents can read arbitrary ticket articles via online notifications
item.description:
CVSS 7.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-639, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
An authenticated agent could read the content of any ticket article in the system, including internal notes and articles in tickets of groups the agent had no access to. The disclosed data comprised the article body, sender and recipient details, and the core data of the related ticket such as title, state, customer and owner. File attachments themselves remained protected.
The prerequisite was an agent account that had received at least one online notification, which happens in normal use. Once exploited, access persisted even after the agent's group permissions or agent role were revoked, until the account was deactivated.
A similar issue allowed agents to see titles and metadata of unpublished knowledge base answers.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Agent sessions disclosed macros and AI text tools of all groups
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Macros and AI text tools could be restricted to specific groups or deactivated. Every agent nevertheless received all macros and AI text tools of the system, including those of groups they had no access to and deactivated ones, with their full configuration: the actions of a macro, which can contain internal note texts and notification email recipients, subjects and bodies, and the prompt of an AI text tool. Deactivated ticket templates and the names of shared drafts in other groups were exposed the same way.
Any agent account was sufficient. The exposure was read-only: the records could not be changed, and macros of other groups still could not be applied.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Remote image tracking and API path bypass via backslash URLs in HTML sanitizer
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:L/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-20, CWE-184, CWE-352
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
The HTML sanitizer did not recognize certain malformed image URLs as pointing to an external host. An unauthenticated attacker who could send an email to a Zammad instance could have embedded images that were loaded when an agent viewed the article, even though external content is blocked. This revealed the agent's IP address, browser user agent and the time the article was read, and no notice about blocked content was shown.
The same weakness could have been used to make the agent's browser request Zammad API endpoints that change state via GET, for example signing the agent out when viewing the article. No ticket data was exposed and no other data could be altered.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Partial admin permissions allowed changing restricted system settings and account takeover
item.description:
CVSS 8.6 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-269, CWE-285
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Users with any partial administrative permission, for example only the permission to manage text modules, could read and change system settings that were meant for full administrators only. This included the developer mode, which allowed logging in to any account with a shared password, as well as the search index connection settings and their credentials.
As a result, such a user could have taken over any account without two-factor authentication configured, including full administrator accounts, and could have redirected indexed ticket data to a server of their choosing.
Installations that do not grant partial administrative permissions to any role or API token were not affected.

item.title: [CRITICAL] zammad/zammad — Unauthenticated creation of administrator accounts during a data migration
item.description:
CVSS 9.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-306
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
While a data migration from another helpdesk system was running, the endpoints for creating the first administrator account during system set-up remained publicly accessible. An unauthenticated attacker who could reach the Zammad instance during this time could have created their own administrator account and thereby gained full control over the system, including all migrated tickets, users and configuration data.
Only installations that were being set up via a migration (import) were affected. The exposure lasted for the duration of the migration, and indefinitely if a migration failed and was not completed. Installations set up without a migration, or whose migration had finished successfully, were not affected.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Session identifier still disclosed through GraphQL session and login responses
item.description:
CVSS 7.4 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:P/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-522
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
The fix for GHSA-23hj-h8w6-rgm3 was incomplete. Zammad's GraphQL API, which serves the new desktop and mobile interfaces, still returned the signed-in user's session identifier in its session and login responses. Scripts running in that user's browser were therefore still able to read it, which the session cookie's `HttpOnly` flag is meant to prevent.
An attacker who had already gained script execution in a user's session, through a separate weakness, could copy the identifier to a machine of their own and act as that user from there for the life of the session, without their password or second factor. This included reading everything the account could see and creating or changing data in the user's name. The reach scaled with the privileges of the affected account.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Memory corruption in Ruby's regular expression compiler via administrator-configured patterns
item.description:
CVSS 8.6 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-190, CWE-415
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Zammad shipped with a Ruby version whose regular expression engine (Onigmo) could corrupt memory while compiling specially crafted patterns. The Ruby project fixed these flaws in Ruby 3.4.12; GitLab reported them as CVE-2026-89078, CVE-2026-93577, CVE-2026-97229 and CVE-2026-110264.
Zammad compiles regular expressions that are configured in Core Workflows, postmaster filters, the monitoring integrations, the CTI integration, the chat channel and some email settings. A user with the matching administrator permission could have entered a crafted pattern that corrupted the memory of the Zammad process. Depending on the pattern, this could have crashed the process or, in the worst case, allowed code execution on the server with the privileges of the Zammad service account. Agents, customers and unauthenticated users could not supply such patterns.
Zammad now uses Ruby 3.4.12. Installations from source must update their Ruby version to 3.4.12 manually. The DEB and RPM packages and the official container images include the updated Ruby version.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Disclosure of internal service responses via external authentication profile images
item.description:
CVSS 6.0 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-345, CWE-918
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When a user logged in through an external authentication provider, Zammad fetched the profile image URL supplied by the provider and stored the response as the user's avatar without checking that it actually was an image. This fetch could also reach services on the internal network and on the Zammad host itself.
A user who could set their own profile image URL at a connected identity provider could have used this to read responses from internal services that do not require authentication, for example a local Elasticsearch instance holding ticket data.
Installations were only affected if they used an external authentication provider that lets users or third parties control the profile image URL. Providers that host profile images themselves were not affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Customers could delete shared ticket drafts prepared by agents
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-639, CWE-862
Affected: - zammad/zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Shared drafts prepared by agents could be deleted by customers who were not allowed to use them. A customer could remove the shared new-ticket drafts of any group while creating a ticket, and the shared reply drafts of tickets they could access as a customer while replying to them. Agents without access to a group could not delete its drafts. Shared drafts are enabled per group by default, and no hard-to-obtain information was needed.
The content of the drafts was not disclosed, and no other ticket data could be read or changed. The effect was limited to the loss of draft text that agents had prepared.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Disclosure of inaccessible tickets via checklist references
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When an agent opened a ticket in the legacy user interface, Zammad also loaded checklists of other tickets that referenced it. If such a checklist belonged to a ticket in a group the agent had no access to, the server still included that ticket in its response, although the user interface did not display it.
This could have allowed an authenticated agent to read the attributes of tickets outside their groups, such as title, note and state, together with details of the related customer, owner and organization, and the checklist items of that ticket. Only tickets whose checklist referenced a ticket the agent could access were exposed. The agent could not choose which tickets to read, and no data could be modified.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Unauthenticated memory exhaustion via crafted image attachments
item.description:
CVSS 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-409, CWE-770
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Zammad generated preview images for incoming JPEG and PNG attachments without limiting the size of the decoded image. A small, specially crafted image file could therefore cause the processing Zammad process to allocate several gigabytes of memory and spend seconds of CPU time per attachment.
No authentication was required: an image attached to an email sent to any address monitored by a Zammad email channel was sufficient. Uploads by logged-in users were affected in the same way. Repeated attempts could exhaust the memory of the server, slowing down or interrupting the processing of emails and web requests. The impact depended on the memory available to the installation. No data could be read or modified.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Overview cache could disclose tickets to users without access
item.description:
CVSS 6.0 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-524, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
The cache used for ticket overviews in the new desktop interface did not take all ticket access rules into account. Users with the same group permissions shared one cache entry, even if they could see different tickets because they were also customers of their own tickets or members of a shared organization.
As a result, an authenticated user could have been shown tickets in an overview that they were not authorized to access. Exposed were the ticket attributes displayed in the overview list, such as number, title, customer and state. The user could not choose which tickets were disclosed.
Affected were installations with users that hold both agent and customer permissions, or with overviews assigned to the Customer role that do not restrict tickets to the current user.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Channel type restriction bypass for partial channel administrators
item.description:
CVSS 7.0 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-639, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Users holding only the permission to manage SMS, Facebook or e-mail channels could have accessed channels of other types, such as e-mail, Microsoft 365, Google, Telegram or WhatsApp channels. The affected endpoints checked the general channel permission, but not whether the requested channel belonged to the channel type the user was allowed to manage.
With the SMS or Facebook channel permission, other channels could have been read, changed, disabled or deleted, while their passwords and access tokens remained masked. With the e-mail channel permission, the stored access token of a Microsoft 365 or Google channel could have been disclosed to the user.
This required an account with one of these partial admin permissions. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Delegated administrators could read stored records and credentials through template placeholders
item.description:
CVSS 8.2 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:H/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-470, CWE-1336
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Users who were permitted to manage only certain configuration areas, without full administrator permissions, could have read data outside their permissions through the placeholders Zammad supports in configurable texts. This included protected system settings such as the application secret, any stored record, and the credentials of configured email accounts. The values could have been made visible in content the user could read, for example an internal ticket note created by a trigger, an inserted text module or a rendered object attribute link.
The attack required an account with the permission to manage triggers, schedulers, macros, text modules, object attributes, AI agents, AI text tools or email channels. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Revoked and refreshed OAuth2 tokens remained usable
item.description:
CVSS 7.6 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-613
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Zammad did not honor the revocation of OAuth2 tokens issued by its OAuth2 provider. An access token that was revoked by its client, or replaced by refreshing it, continued to be accepted for API requests until its regular expiry, by default up to two hours. A refresh token that had already been used to obtain a new access token was never revoked and could be used again to obtain further access tokens, without any time limit.
Anyone in possession of such a token, for example after it had leaked, could therefore keep reading and changing all data with the permissions of the user the token was issued for, in the case of a refresh token even after the client had already refreshed it. Installations that do not use OAuth2 applications were not affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Remote content and API path bypass via inline styles in HTML sanitizer
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:L/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-184, CWE-352
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
The HTML sanitizer did not check the value of a background style that is allowed on some text and table elements. A specially crafted email or article could therefore have made the browser of an agent opening it load content from a foreign server, although loading of external content was blocked and no notice about blocked content was shown. The sender could have learned the agent's IP address, browser and time of reading.
The same weakness could have caused the agent's browser to request certain Zammad API endpoints in the agent's own session, for example ending that session.
No Zammad account was required; sending an email to a monitored address was enough.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Partial administrators could replace the product logo
item.description:
CVSS 5.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
An authenticated user with permission to change at least one system setting, but without the branding permission, could have replaced the product logo of the Zammad system. The authorization check of the logo upload was performed against a setting chosen by the caller instead of the logo setting itself.
The replaced logo was shown to all users, including customers on the login page, and could have been used to make the system look defaced or to support phishing attempts. No data was disclosed and no other setting could be changed this way. Installations in which only full administrators hold any admin permission were not affected.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — Customers kept receiving live updates of shared-organization tickets after leaving the organization
item.description:
CVSS 2.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-613, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Real-time GraphQL subscriptions kept using the authorization state a user had when their browser connection was opened. When a customer was moved out of a shared organization while still connected, subscriptions they had already opened for tickets of that organization continued to receive updates, such as ticket title, state and newly added public articles, even though regular requests correctly denied access.
The exposure was limited to tickets the customer had already subscribed to before the change, applied only to organizations with shared ticket access, and ended as soon as the connection was re-established. It was read-only. Installations where customers do not change organizations, or that do not use shared organizations, were not affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Missing limit on failed two-factor attempts allows brute-forcing the second factor
item.description:
CVSS 6.0 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-307
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Failed two-factor authentication attempts at login were neither counted towards the account lockout nor rate limited, and users were not notified about them. An attacker who already knew a user's password could therefore keep guessing the one-time code of the authenticator app method without ever being locked out.
A successful guess required sustained effort over days per account, but several accounts could be targeted in parallel. It gave full access to the affected account with that user's permissions, including all tickets and customer data the user could see.
Only accounts using the authenticator app method were affected. Security keys and recovery codes could not be guessed this way.

item.title: [CRITICAL] zammad/zammad — Encrypted or signed incoming email could reintroduce privileged headers past the untrusted-mail filter
item.description:
CVSS 9.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-345, CWE-501, CWE-639
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When the S/MIME or PGP integration was enabled, Zammad could take internal control headers from the content of encrypted incoming emails, and of certain signed S/MIME emails, although it removes these headers from mail received through untrusted channels. An unauthenticated remote sender could use this to add articles to existing tickets, have them recorded as written by another user, and change ticket attributes such as owner, group, state and customer. By assigning a ticket to a customer account they controlled, an attacker could also gain access to its content and attachments in the customer portal.
Exploitation required an active S/MIME or PGP integration. Neither a trusted certificate nor a valid signature was needed: for encrypted mail, the publicly distributed certificate or key of a Zammad email address was enough.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — Live updates of macros and AI text tools disclosed their identifiers and group assignments to all logged-in users
item.description:
CVSS 2.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Zammad sent live updates about macros and AI text tools to every logged-in user, regardless of their permissions. Whenever one of these records was created, changed or deleted, all open sessions received its internal identifier and the identifiers of the groups it was assigned to. Customers were included, although macros and AI text tools are not available to them at all.
Receiving this data required nothing beyond a logged-in account; the identifiers arrived on their own as soon as someone changed such a record.
The disclosure was limited to identifiers and group assignments. The name of a macro, the actions it performs, the instructions behind an AI text tool and any ticket or customer data were not included, and nothing could be changed. Installations in which only agents and administrators hold accounts were not affected.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Disclosure of user profile data to customer-privileged accounts via the ticket creation form
item.description:
CVSS 7.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-639
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When the ticket creation form was opened for a particular customer, Zammad returned that account's stored profile data without checking whether the requesting user was allowed to see it. The request was accepted from accounts holding only customer permissions, and the account it referred to could be freely chosen, so a single low-privileged account could have read the profile of every user on the instance, including agents and administrators.
The data returned covered first and last name, email address, telephone and mobile number, VIP status and out-of-office periods, together with the name, domain and VIP status of the account's organization. Passwords, tokens and ticket content were not reachable this way, and nothing could be modified.
On instances where self-registration was enabled, anyone able to create an account was in a position to do this; elsewhere it required an existing customer account.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — AI-generated knowledge base drafts could be saved into categories the agent was not allowed to edit
item.description:
CVSS 2.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-862, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad >= 7.1.0, <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When AI assistance generated a knowledge base answer draft from a ticket, the category it was filed under was not checked against the acting agent's permissions. An agent with editor permission on at least one category could therefore end up with a new draft in a category they were only allowed to read, or could not access at all. Creating the same answer manually was correctly refused. Existing answers could not be changed this way.
The drafts were unpublished and tagged as AI-generated, so nothing became publicly visible on its own.
Only installations with an AI provider configured, knowledge base draft generation enabled and per-category editor permissions were affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Denial of Service via Unauthenticated Websocket Message
item.description:
CVSS 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:N/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-20, CWE-248
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Zammad's websocket server could be terminated by a single message from an unauthenticated client. Incoming messages were accepted and processed before any authentication took place, and a message that did not have the expected structure was not rejected but ended the process instead.
While the service was down, real-time updates in the classic agent interface stopped and the Zammad Chat widget on public websites was unavailable. Ticket handling over HTTP continued to work, and no data could be read or changed. The service restarted automatically in most deployments, but the message could be repeated at will, and on systemd installations the default restart limit could leave the service stopped until an administrator intervened.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — Maintenance mode was not enforced on real-time connections
item.description:
CVSS 2.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-613, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
While maintenance mode was active, Zammad denied access to all users without the maintenance permission. The real-time connections that the browser uses did not apply that check consistently, and a user's session stayed valid after their requests had been refused. Logging such a user out was left to their client; where that did not happen, the user could have continued to read and change data over these connections for as long as maintenance mode stayed active.
The user kept only their regular permissions: they could not access any ticket, customer or setting beyond what their role and group access already allowed. Installations were only affected while maintenance mode was enabled.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Partial administrators could add unchecked options to system settings
item.description:
CVSS 5.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-470, CWE-915
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Administrators with a partial administrative permission, for example only the permission for security settings, could store additional internal options on the system settings they were allowed to change. The server acted on these options.
This could have been used to hide a setting from all administrators, including full administrators, so that it could no longer be viewed or changed through the user interface or API, and to make the server run internal code components chosen by the attacker whenever the setting was saved.
Exploitation required an authenticated account with at least one administrative permission that grants access to a system setting. Installations where only fully trusted users hold administrative permissions were not exposed to other users.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Partial administrators could delete records and read restricted data via core workflow conditions
item.description:
CVSS 8.6 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-470, CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Administrators with only the permission to manage core workflows could configure a workflow condition that made the server call internal functions on the record being evaluated, instead of only reading its fields. The condition ran whenever the workflow was evaluated, which happens when any user, including customers, opens, changes or saves a form it applies to.
This could have been used to delete tickets, users or other records, actions reserved for other administrative permissions, and to read data the administrator was not allowed to see, such as fields hidden from them and other users' API tokens, including those of full administrators.
Exploitation required an authenticated account with the core workflow administration permission. Installations where only fully trusted users hold this permission were not exposed.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Administrators could replace internal components of system settings, incl. password authentication
item.description:
CVSS 5.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-470
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
### Impact
Several system settings store the name of an internal server component that Zammad loads and runs, for example the backends for password authentication, ticket numbering, dashboard statistics and external services. The server did not check that a saved value named a component intended for that setting.
An administrator with the permission for one of these settings could have chosen a different component. For the password authentication settings, this could have made Zammad accept any password for every account without two-factor authentication configured, including administrator accounts. This change was not visible in the admin interface and stayed in effect after the permission was revoked. For the other settings, the affected feature could have been made to fail.
Exploitation required an authenticated account with an administrative permission for one of these settings. Installations where only fully trusted users hold administrative permissions were not exposed to other users.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — Knowledge base search showed answers from restricted categories to editors
item.description:
CVSS 2.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:H/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When knowledge base categories were restricted per role, users who could edit the knowledge base could still find answers and categories in the knowledge base search that their role had no access to. This also happened during a normal search on the public help site while logged in.
The results included answer titles, short excerpts or matching fragments of the answer content, tags and category titles, also for draft, internal and archived answers. The full answer could not be opened.
Only installations that use per-category knowledge base permissions to restrict users who can edit the knowledge base were affected. Read-only users and customers were not affected. This was a second path to the weakness described in GHSA-4m54-p3mr-22g2, which the earlier fix did not cover.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Cross-site request forgery in realtime update endpoint
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:N/UI:P/VC:N/VI:L/VA:L/SC:N/SI:L/SA:L) · CWE-352
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
One of the endpoints used for realtime updates in the web interface was not protected against cross-site request forgery. A third-party website visited by a logged-in Zammad user could have caused that user's browser to trigger realtime actions in the user's name, without the user's knowledge.
The impact depended on the permissions of the affected user. For users with permission to manage maintenance, it could have sent maintenance messages or a forced page reload to all connected users, for example to show a misleading message. For other users, it could have disrupted their own open sessions or changed their chat availability. No data was disclosed to the attacker.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — HTML injection in WhatsApp reaction notification emails
item.description:
CVSS 2.1 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:A/VC:N/VI:N/VA:N/SC:L/SI:L/SA:N) · CWE-79, CWE-80
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Email notifications about reactions to WhatsApp messages did not escape the reacting contact's display name and reaction before inserting them into the HTML email sent to agents.
Any WhatsApp contact could therefore place HTML markup into Zammad notification emails received by agents, without needing an account or any permission in Zammad. This could have been used to make a trusted notification email show spoofed content, phishing links or forms, or remote images that reveal when and where the email was opened. Script execution in Zammad itself was not possible, and no ticket data was exposed.
Only installations with an active WhatsApp channel were affected, and only agents who receive email notifications for ticket updates. The actual effect depended on how the agent's email client handled HTML content.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Delegated text module and trigger managers could read protected system settings
item.description:
CVSS 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Users who were permitted to manage only text modules or triggers, without full administrator permissions, could have read protected system settings that are reserved for administrators. These included the application secret and credentials stored in the system configuration, such as the Elasticsearch and proxy passwords and the client secrets of configured third-party login providers. The values could have been made visible in content that the user could read, for example an inserted text module or an internal ticket note created by a trigger.
The attack required an account with the text module (together with agent access) or the trigger administration permission. Installations that grant these permissions only to full administrators were not affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — API token permission restrictions not applied to live update pushes
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Personal access tokens can be limited to a subset of their owner's permissions. Zammad did not apply this limit to the live updates it pushed through one of its browser connection channels. Anyone holding a restricted token could have used it to receive the owner's ticket overview lists and activity stream, including ticket metadata and the names and contact details of the users and organizations involved, even if the token itself had no ticket permissions.
Exploitation required possession of a valid token of an agent or customer account. Access was read-only and limited to data the token owner could see in their overviews and activity stream; ticket article content was not exposed. Installations where API token access is disabled were not affected.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Account takeover via client-controlled identity in SSO authentication
item.description:
CVSS 7.7 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-290, CWE-348
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
In installations with SSO authentication enabled, Zammad accepted the user identity from more than one source, and a source that the client could control took precedence over the identity set by the authenticating reverse proxy. The reverse proxy configurations shipped with Zammad and the documented SSO setup did not remove this client-controlled value.
This could have allowed a user who was able to reach the SSO endpoint through the proxy, for example any user authenticated against the directory service, to log in as any other Zammad user, including administrators, and to read and modify all data accessible to that user.
Only installations with SSO authentication enabled were affected. Restricting SSO to trusted proxy IP addresses did not prevent this. Administrators who cannot update immediately should make sure their reverse proxy removes the `Remote-User` request header from incoming client requests.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Sender identity spoofing via headers inside encrypted or signed emails
item.description:
CVSS 6.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:N/VI:L/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-290, CWE-345
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When the S/MIME or PGP integration was enabled, an unauthenticated remote sender could make an incoming email appear to originate from a different address. By placing a forged sender inside encrypted content, or inside a signed message with an untrusted signature, the resulting ticket or article could be attributed to another existing customer, an agent, or a system address, including that user's account.
Sender authentication performed by the mail infrastructure, such as SPF, DKIM or DMARC, did not prevent this. Agents could be misled into acting on requests that seemingly came from a trusted person. Installations without S/MIME or PGP integration enabled were not affected.

item.title: [LOW] zammad/zammad — Agents could receive ticket notifications shortly after role-based group access was revoked
item.description:
CVSS 2.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:H/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-863
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
After an agent lost access to a group through a role change, Zammad could still send that agent ticket notifications for that group for up to 20 seconds. This applied when a role was removed from the agent, when a group was removed from one of the agent's roles, or when such a role was deactivated. Removing a group directly from the agent was not affected.
During this window, the agent could receive online and email notifications for tickets in the group they could no longer access. These notifications could contain the ticket title, the changed ticket attributes, and the article content including inline attachments. The agent could neither trigger such notifications nor choose the ticket; only tickets that were updated by others within the window were exposed.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Customer ticket search matches content of internal articles
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-203
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Ticket search for customers did not exclude data that is visible to agents only. While customers could only find their own tickets and tickets of organizations they share, the search term was also compared against internal articles, their attachments and other agent-only ticket information.
An authenticated customer could therefore find out whether such internal content on their own or their organization's tickets contained a chosen term, for example a name or an amount, by observing which tickets were returned. The content itself was never displayed. Installations using Elasticsearch were affected to a larger extent, as more agent-only ticket information was included in the search there.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — AI-generated ticket field values could disclose protected system settings
item.description:
CVSS 6.0 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-200, CWE-1336
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
When an AI agent that writes AI-generated text into ticket fields was enabled, such as the "Ticket Title Rewriter", a customer could craft the content of a ticket so that the generated value was processed as a template on the server. This could have caused protected system settings, such as the application secret and credentials stored for configured integrations and the AI provider, to be written into a ticket field the customer could read, for example the ticket title.
The attack required an AI provider and such an AI agent to be configured by an administrator, and it depended on the language model following instructions embedded in the ticket content. Installations without AI agents were not affected.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — GitLab API token stored in clear text in the HTTP log
item.description:
CVSS 6.9 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:N/PR:H/UI:N/VC:H/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-532
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
Requests of the GitLab integration were recorded in the HTTP log with the GitLab API token in clear text, because the masking of sensitive values did not cover the way this integration sends its token.
Users with permission to view the integration logs (`admin.integration`) could therefore read the stored GitLab API token, although the integration settings hide it from them. With the token, they could access the connected GitLab instance within the token's scopes.
Only installations with the GitLab integration enabled were affected. Log entries written before the update may still contain the token, so administrators should rotate the GitLab API token after upgrading.

item.title: [MEDIUM] zammad/zammad — Public knowledge base feed disclosed titles of non-public categories
item.description:
CVSS 6.3 (CVSS:4.0/AV:N/AC:L/AT:P/PR:N/UI:N/VC:L/VI:N/VA:N/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-862
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.2 (patched: 7.2.3)
---
The public knowledge base feed of a category did not check whether the category was meant to be visible on the public help center. An unauthenticated visitor could have read the titles of categories that contained only internal or draft answers, and therefore stay hidden on the public help center. Because category identifiers are sequential, all such titles could have been collected, and the responses also revealed which categories existed.
The contents of internal or draft answers were not exposed; the feed only ever listed published answers. No data could be modified.
Only installations with an active knowledge base were affected, and only if it contained categories without published answers. How sensitive this is depends on what the category titles of such a knowledge base reveal.

item.title: [MEDIUM] composer/composer — Inline repository HTTP credentials sent to attacker controlled dist mirrors supplied in `composer.lock` / `installed.json`
item.description:
CVSS 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) · CWE-200, CWE-522
Affected: - composer/composer/composer >= 2.11.0, < 2.11.2 (patched: 2.11.2) - composer/composer/composer >= 2.2.31, < 2.2.32 (patched: 2.2.32)
---
## Summary
For projects that authenticate to a Composer repository using an inline HTTP header credential, a crafted `composer.lock` or `vendor/composer/installed.json` could cause that credential to be sent to a download mirror on an attacker-controlled host during `composer install`. This is an information disclosure issue limited to that repository credential. There is no code execution and no file modification.
## Am I affected?
You are affected if all of the following hold:
- You run Composer 2.11.0, 2.11.1, or 2.2.31. - You configure a Composer repository with an inline HTTP header that carries a secret, for example an `Authorization` bearer token or an API key set in the repository's options (common with Private Packagist and Satis-style setups). - An attacker can influence your `composer.lock` or `vendor/composer/installed.json`, for example through a pull request that edits the lock file, a committed lock in a shared project, or a poisoned CI cache.
When those hold, a crafted entry can add a preferred download mirror pointing at a host the attacker controls, and the repository credential is then sent to that host.
You are plainly not affected if your repositories do not use an inline header credential, or if you are on a release that does not re-attach repository headers at load time (any version other than 2.11.0, 2.11.1, and 2.2.31).
## Patched versions
Fixed in 2.11.2 and 2.2.32.
## Workarounds
The only complete fix is upgrading.

item.title: [HIGH] composer/composer — Arbitrary file write outside the package directory via symlinked zip entries and the `unzip` to `ZipArchive` extraction fallback
item.description:
CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) · CWE-22, CWE-59
Affected: - composer/composer/composer >= 2.3.0, < 2.11.2 (patched: 2.11.2) - composer/composer/composer >= 1.0, < 2.2.32 (patched: 2.2.32)
---
## Summary
A malicious package archive could cause Composer to write a file outside the intended package directory during `composer install`, `composer update`, or `composer require`. Because the written file can be an application entry point or another file that later gets executed, this can lead to code execution. It is arbitrary file write, not a flaw triggered by normal Packagist-hosted packages, which do not carry the kind of archive entries required.
## Am I affected?
You are affected if all of the following hold:
- You run Composer 1.0.0 through 2.11.1. - You install packages whose distribution archive (zip) an attacker can control. In practice this means untrusted third-party Composer repositories, private or self-hosted repositories, artifact mirrors, or any attacker-controlled dist URL. - Your system has the `unzip` command available (standard on Linux and macOS) together with the PHP zip extension.
When those hold, a crafted archive can redirect one of its entries so the content lands outside the package directory, for example overwriting a front controller in the project root, which yields code execution on the next request or command.
You are plainly not affected if every package you install comes from a trusted source. Packagist.org-hosted archives generally do not contain the archive entries this relies on, so typical Packagist.org-only installs are not a realistic vector.
The single most realistic way to get hit: adding or updating a package served by an untrusted or attacker-controlled repository or mirror.
## Patched versions
Fixed in 2.11.2 and 2.2.32.
## Workarounds
The only complete fix is upgrading.

item.title: [HIGH] composer/composer — Arbitrary command execution via `transport-options.prevent_url_access_callable` loaded from `composer.lock` / `installed.json`
item.description:
CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) · CWE-78, CWE-470
Affected: - composer/composer/composer >= 2.10.0, < 2.11.2 (patched: 2.11.2)
---
## Summary
A crafted `composer.lock` or `vendor/composer/installed.json` could cause Composer to run an arbitrary system command while resolving downloads during `composer install` or `composer update`. This is data-driven arbitrary command execution: it does not require a malicious package to be installed or any package code to run, only the ability to influence those two files, and the command runs before any checksum or integrity check. It is not a flaw in how trusted package code executes.
## Am I affected?
You are affected if all of the following hold:
- You run Composer 2.10.0 through 2.11.1. - You run `composer install` or `composer update` against a `composer.lock` or `vendor/composer/installed.json` whose contents an attacker could influence.
Realistic ways that file becomes attacker-influenced include a pull request that only edits `composer.lock`, a shared or scaffolded project template that ships a lock file, a compromised dependency-update bot, or a CI cache that restores a poisoned lock or installed file.
You are plainly not affected if nothing untrusted can modify your lock or installed-packages files, or if you are on the 2.2 LTS line (or any release before 2.10.0), which never had the affected option handling.
The single most realistic way to get hit: automated CI that checks out a branch and runs `composer install` without a human reviewing the lock-file change. `--no-scripts` and `--no-plugins` do not prevent it.
## Patched versions
Fixed in 2.11.2. The fix makes Composer ignore these download-time callback options when they come from the lock or installed-packages file, and only honor them when they are set programmatically.
## Workarounds
The only complete fix is upgrading. To reduce risk until then, do not run `composer install`/`update` on lock or installed files from untrusted sources (unreviewed pull requests outside of CI running sandboxed, third-party templates, shared caches).

item.title: [MEDIUM] composer/composer — Inline repository HTTP headers, such as API tokens, are written into composer.lock
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N) · CWE-200
Affected: - composer/composer/composer >= 2.3.0, < 2.11.0 (patched: 2.11.0) - composer/composer/composer >= 1.0, < 2.2.31 (patched: 2.2.31)
---
## Summary
When a Composer repository is configured with inline HTTP headers (the `options.http.header` setting of a `composer` type repository), Composer copied those headers into `composer.lock` for every package downloaded from that repository. Such headers usually carry an API token or another credential, and `composer.lock` is usually committed to version control, so the credential could end up stored in places it was never meant to be.
This is an information disclosure issue. It cannot be triggered by a malicious package or a remote party. Whether a credential was actually exposed depends on who can read the lock file.
## Am I affected?
You are exposed if all of the following are true:
- You use a `composer` type repository with `options.http.header` set (the "inline custom headers" authentication method). - That repository is defined outside the project's `composer.json`, typically in your global `config.json` (for example via `composer config --global`), so the project itself does not otherwise contain the credential. - Package archives are downloaded from under that repository's URL, which is common for private Composer repositories. - The generated `composer.lock` is shared with people or systems that should not have the credential, for example by committing it to a repository, publishing it as a build artifact or attaching it to a bug report.
If the inline header is defined in the project's `composer.json`, it is also copied into `composer.lock`, but the credential is already in the committed `composer.json`, so the lock file adds no new exposure.
You are **not** affected if your credentials are stored in `auth.json` or the `COMPOSER_AUTH` environment variable (`http-basic`, `bearer`, `custom-headers`, `github-oauth` and similar). Those were never written to `composer.lock`.
The most likely way to be affected: a developer machine or CI worker has a private repository with a token header in its global `config.json`, runs `composer update`, and the resulting `composer.lock` is committed.
## Patched versions
Composer no longer writes repository HTTP headers into `composer.lock`. When installing from a lock file, headers are taken from the currently configured repositories instead, so header based authentication keeps working.
Fixed in Composer 2.11.0 and 2.2.31 (LTS).
Existing lock files keep any headers they already contain until they are rewritten. After upgrading, run `composer update --lock` (or any update) to rewrite the lock file without them.
## Workarounds
Upgrading is the fix. Until you can upgrade:
- If your repository supports it, store the credential in `auth.json` instead of an inline header, for example as `bearer`, `http-basic`, or `custom-headers` on Composer versions that support it. - Check `composer.lock` for `header` entries under `transport-options` before committing or sharing it.
## If you may have been affected
Search your repositories' history for `composer.lock` files containing `header` entries under `transport-options`. If a credential appears in a lock file that was shared, revoke and rotate it. Removing it from the latest commit does not remove it from the history.

item.title: [HIGH] composer/composer — Package names in vendor/composer/installed.json can escape the vendor directory during install and reinstall
item.description:
CVSS 7.1 (CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:N/I:H/A:H) · CWE-22
Affected: - composer/composer/composer >= 2.3.0, < 2.11.0 (patched: 2.11.0) - composer/composer/composer >= 1.0, < 2.2.31 (patched: 2.2.31)
---
## Summary
Composer did not validate the package names recorded in `vendor/composer/installed.json`. A crafted entry whose name contains `..` path segments made Composer delete a directory outside of `vendor/` during `composer install`, and on `composer reinstall` also write the package's files there. Malicious names in `composer.lock` and in repository metadata were already rejected; only the locally recorded package list was trusted.
This is arbitrary file deletion and file write with the privileges of the user running Composer. It is not exploitable remotely and cannot be triggered by publishing a package: the attacker has to be able to write to `vendor/composer/installed.json` on the machine running Composer.
## Am I affected?
You can only be exposed to this if the vendor directory (specifically `vendor/composer/installed.json`) was not produced by a trusted Composer run on this machine. For example it was restored from a shared or untrusted CI cache, copied in from another container build stage or artifact, or is writable by a lower-trust step of your build.
You are not affected if your `vendor/` directory is only ever created and modified by Composer runs you trust, which is the case for most local development setups.
The most realistic scenario is a CI pipeline that restores `vendor/` from a cache that untrusted jobs (for example pull requests from forks) can also write to.
## Patched versions
Composer now validates locally installed packages the same way it validates resolved and locked packages, and aborts before performing any operation if an invalid package is found.
Fixed in Composer 2.11.0 and 2.2.31 (LTS).

item.title: [MEDIUM] icinga/icinga2 — /v1/objects: supposedly inaccessible related objects can be accessed in filter expressions
item.description:
CVSS 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) · CWE-200
Affected: - Icinga 2 <= v2.16.5, <= v2.15.6 (patched: v2.16.6, v2.15.7)
---
### Impact
Authenticated API users with access to the `/v1/objects` API endpoint may, under certain conditions, access objects in filter expressions they are not otherwise permitted to access. The access is limited to objects related to objects the user is allowed to access, so for example, if an API user is granted only the `objects/query/Service` permission, they cannot retrieve information about other object types from the API. However, their filter expressions are executed in a scope that may have contained references to objects not accessible otherwise. This only grants access to related objects like the `Host` the `Service` belongs to or its `CheckCommand`, not arbitrary objects.
### Patches
The following versions of Icinga 2 include fixes for this vulnerability: v2.16.6, v2.15.7.
### Workarounds
This issue can only be mitigated by stopping malicious users from using filter expressions in `/v1/objects`, either by disabling access for untrusted `ApiUser` objects or by limiting their access by [enabling enforcement of the recently added `filter-expression`](https://icinga.com/docs/icinga-2/latest/doc/16-upgrading-icinga-2/#new-filter-expression-permission) permission and not granting it to untrusted `ApiUser` objects.
### References
* [Release Announcement](https://icinga.com/blog/icinga-2-v2-16-6-and-icinga-web-v2-14-1/) * [PR with the patch](https://github.com/Icinga/icinga2/pull/11146)

item.title: [MEDIUM] icinga/icinga2 — Multiple instances of log injections
item.description:
CVSS 5.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) · CWE-117
Affected: - Icinga 2 <= v2.16.5, <= v2.15.6 (patched: v2.16.6, v2.15.7)
---
### Impact
There are multiple instances in Icinga 2 where values inserted into log messages are not properly sanitized, allowing an attacker to falsify logs. This mostly affects `FileLogger` and `CompatLogger`, but other loggers could be affected as well, depending on how downstream systems processing the log messages are configured. The injections can originate from values like certificate common names, command outputs, user comments, HTTP responses, and JSON-RPC inputs, some of which can be influenced by an unauthenticated attacker.
### Patches
The following versions of Icinga 2 include fixes for this vulnerability: v2.16.6, v2.15.7.
The fixes are twofold: For the aforementioned values, explicit quoting and escaping of the values inserted is added. As a second line of defense, all log messages now undergo some basic sanitization escaping ASCII control characters and indenting all but the first line of multi-line messages, so that lines are clearly marked as a continuation of the previous line.
### Workarounds
Logging using a method that is able to handle multi-line messages natively (like for example systemd journald via [`JournaldLogger`](https://icinga.com/docs/icinga-2/latest/doc/09-object-types/#journaldlogger) prevents the injection of full log lines.
### References
* [Release Announcement](https://icinga.com/blog/icinga-2-v2-16-6-and-icinga-web-v2-14-1/) * [PR with the patch](https://github.com/Icinga/icinga2/pull/11147)

item.title: [MEDIUM] icinga/icinga2 — Attacker-Controlled Comparator crashes Array#sort
item.description:
Affected: - Icinga 2 >=v2.3.0, <=v2.16.5, <=v2.15.6 (patched: v2.16.6, v2.15.7)
---
### Impact
If an attacker can call the Icinga 2 DSL `Array#sort` function, they can provide a custom comparison function that does not follow a strict weak ordering. This can crash Icinga 2 with a segmentation fault.
The most critical way to exploit this is via a crafted filter expression run against one of the API endpoints that supports the `filter` parameter, like `/v1/objects` or `/v1/actions`.
### Patches
The following versions of Icinga 2 include fixes for this vulnerability: v2.16.6, v2.15.7.
### Workarounds
This issue can only be mitigated by stopping malicious users from using filter expressions on any API endpoints by [enabling enforcement of the recently added `filter-expression`](https://icinga.com/docs/icinga-2/latest/doc/16-upgrading-icinga-2/#new-filter-expression-permission) permission and not granting it to untrusted `ApiUser` objects.
### References
* [Release Announcement](https://icinga.com/blog/icinga-2-v2-16-6-and-icinga-web-v2-14-1/) * [PR with the patch](https://github.com/Icinga/icinga2/pull/11141)

item.title: [MEDIUM] icinga/icinga2 — The default email notification scripts may allow command injection from the recipient address
item.description:
CVSS 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) · CWE-77
Affected: - Icinga 2 <= v2.16.5, <= v2.15.6 (patched: v2.16.6, v2.15.7)
---
### Impact
The default `mail-host-notification.sh` and `mail-service-notification.sh` notification scripts shipped with Icinga 2 did not sufficiently validate the argument for the recipient address, allowing an attacker to pass arbitrary command line flags to the `mail` binary on the system. The exact impact depends on the implementation of the `mail` binary used on the specific system, in the case of GNU mailutils, there are flags that can be used to execute arbitrary commands.
In order to exploit this, an attacker needs to be able to specify the email address of a `User` object in the Icinga 2 config, for example because they have access to an `ApiUser` with the `objects/modify/User` permission. In that case, they can provide command line flags for the `mail` binary instead of or in addition to a recipient email address. For GNU mailutils, there exists the `--exec` command line flag that can be used to instruct it to execute an arbitrary command. With other `mail` implementations, there could be undesirable effects.
### Patches
The following versions of Icinga 2 include fixes for this vulnerability: v2.16.6, v2.15.7.
**Important:** As the vulnerable script is located in `/etc/icinga2/scripts`, it is treated as a configuration files by package managers and may not be updated automatically if it was modified locally. After upgrading, please verify the fix has been applied (see Workarounds section below) and there are no `*.rpmnew` or `*.dpkg-dist` files in that directory, indicating a newer upstream version.
### Workarounds
The vulnerability exists in scripts shipped in the default configuration in `/etc/icinga2/scripts`, so the fix for this issue can be applied locally without having to upgrade the Icinga 2 packages. To do so, apply the changes from [TODO: link commit] to the files `mail-host-notification.sh` and `mail-service-notification.sh` in that directory.
### References
* [Release Announcement](https://icinga.com/blog/icinga-2-v2-16-6-and-icinga-web-v2-14-1/) * [PR with the patch](https://github.com/Icinga/icinga2/pull/11144)

item.title: [HIGH] espocrm/espocrm — Stored XSS in Knowledge Base articles letting run JS code on link click
item.description:
CVSS 7.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:N) · CWE-79
Affected: - EspoCRM <= 10.0.8 (patched: 10.0.9) - EspoCRM <= 9.3.10 (patched: 9.3.11)
---
## Summary

item.title: [MEDIUM] open-webui/open-webui — Channel members can post messages shown as a webhook via client-supplied message metadata
item.description:
CVSS 4.3 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N) · CWE-290, CWE-345, CWE-863
Affected: - pip/open-webui >= 0.7.0, < 0.12.2 (patched: 0.12.2)
---
# Channel members can post messages shown as a webhook via client-supplied message metadata
## Summary Any member who can post in a channel can make their message appear as if a real webhook of that channel posted it. The server stored the metadata the client sent with a message without checking it. The channel then showed the message under the webhook's name and role, with no webhook token required.
## Preconditions Channels are enabled (`ENABLE_CHANNELS`, default `False`). The channel has at least one webhook. The attacker is a member with write access to the channel. The attacker knows the webhook's id. Any member can read it from a message the webhook posted, so it is not a secret. Instances with channels disabled, or without channel webhooks, are not affected.
## Impact A member can post, edit and pin messages that other members see as coming from a trusted webhook, such as an alerting or ops bot. That makes social engineering inside the channel easy. The stored author is still the attacker's account. The attacker cannot change the webhook's real messages, read anything new or act with the webhook's token.
## Fix Fixed in #32421. The server now drops any message metadata sent by the client, both when a message is posted and when it is edited, so only the server sets it. Upgrading is enough.
## Root cause Component: the channel message post and edit endpoints in `backend/open_webui/routers/channels.py`. Affected setup: every build with channel webhooks, from 0.7.0. The message form accepted an arbitrary metadata object from the client and stored it as is. The message list and the pinned list then trusted that metadata to decide who the message was from. A webhook id in the metadata was enough for the message to be shown as that webhook.
## Proof of concept 1. Admin creates a webhook "Ops Bot" in a channel, and the webhook posts a message. 2. Alice, a channel member, reads the webhook id from that message. 3. Alice posts a message with `meta.webhook = {"id": "<webhook id>", "name": "Ops Bot"}` and pins it. 4. Bob opens the channel. The message and the pinned list show it as `Ops Bot` with role `webhook`, while the stored author is Alice.
Run by the reporter on 0.11.3.
## Credits @Tarekinh0 (reporter)

item.title: [CRITICAL] go:github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2 — Argo CD: AppProject destination-namespace and resource restrictions bypassed by PreDelete/PostDelete resource hooks (CVE-2026-77459)
item.description:
CVE-2026-77459 · CVSS 9.9 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:C/C:H/I:H/A:H) · CWE-863
Affected: - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2 >= 2.10.0, <= 2.14.21 - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.0.0, < 3.3.15 (patched: 3.3.15) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.4.0, < 3.4.10 (patched: 3.4.10) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.5.0, < 3.5.4 (patched: 3.5.4) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.6.0-rc1, < 3.6.0-rc2 (patched: 3.6.0-rc2)
---
### Impact
Argo CD checks an Application's AppProject before it creates resources during a sync. That check covers destination namespaces and servers, cluster-scoped resource allow and deny lists, and namespaced resource allow and deny lists, including resource names. PreDelete and PostDelete hooks skip it. When the Application is deleted, Argo CD creates those hooks with the application-controller's credentials on the destination cluster.
All versions from v2.10.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.9.22 and earlier are not. PostDelete hooks were introduced in [dcc17f70bf](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/dcc17f70bf7db973fe480b8b613189b2c5ac4b4b) (2023-12-18, [#16595](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/16595)) and first released in v2.10.0. That creation path has never applied the project check. PreDelete hooks, added in [3bf3d8a212](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/3bf3d8a2124e772ac651f3fd42375c4e9b8008af) (2025-12-05, [#22288](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/22288)) and first released in v3.3.0, use the same path. v3.2.12 and earlier do not have PreDelete hooks. PreSync, Sync, PostSync, and SyncFail hooks still go through the project check.
A user who can push to the Git repository an Application syncs from can commit a hook whose namespace, group, kind, or name the AppProject would refuse on sync. The controller adds the delete finalizer when it sees the hook, and the Application stays Synced until someone deletes it. Deleting the Application creates the hook. What that can reach is bounded by the application-controller's access to the destination cluster. In a typical install that access is broad, so a tenant can create a cluster-scoped object such as a `ClusterRoleBinding`, or an object in a namespace the project does not allow. A hook with no deletion policy is removed after it succeeds. A deletion policy that does not remove the hook on success leaves the object in the cluster. A hook such as a Job can create further objects that Argo CD does not clean up.
### Patches
A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:
* v3.6.0-rc2 * v3.5.4 * v3.4.10 * v3.3.15
The fix applies the same AppProject destination and resource checks used on sync before creating a PreDelete or PostDelete hook.
Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.
### Workarounds
There is no configuration setting that applies the project check to delete hooks while those hooks stay in use.
* Do not grant untrusted users write access to Git repositories that back Applications in restrictive AppProjects. * Limit who can delete Applications. Deletion is what runs PreDelete and PostDelete hooks. * Tighten the application-controller's Kubernetes access so a hook cannot reach sensitive namespaces or APIs.
### Credits
The Argo CD team would like to thank @RealFakeAccount, @AdamKorcz, @0xshylines, @thevilledev, @HenriWilliams, @cherez0ff, @ARSB1, and @zwindler for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).
### References

item.title: [HIGH] go:github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2 — Argo CD repo-server command injection via crafted SSH repository SOCKS5 proxy URL (CVE-2026-55797)
item.description:
CVE-2026-55797 · CVSS 8.8 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H) · CWE-78
Affected: - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v2 >= 2.11.0, <= 2.14.21 - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.0.0, < 3.3.15 (patched: 3.3.15) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.4.0, < 3.4.10 (patched: 3.4.10) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.5.0, < 3.5.4 (patched: 3.5.4) - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 = 3.6.0-rc1 (patched: 3.6.0-rc2)

### Impact
Argo CD runs a shell command in the repo-server when it clones or fetches an SSH Git repository that has a proxy URL. The proxy host and port are copied into an SSH `ProxyCommand`. A host that contains shell metacharacters breaks out of that command and runs in the repo-server.
All versions from v2.11.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v2.10.20 and earlier are not. The behavior was introduced in [9b27aeb1a4](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/9b27aeb1a4fb15d11a0f01cad65dea1fdfc60205) (2024-01-09, [#15864](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/15864)), the change that added SOCKS5 proxy support for SSH Git URLs, and was first released in v2.11.0.
The repository must use SSH. `http`, `https`, and `socks5` proxy URLs all take this path when they are set on an SSH repository. An HTTPS Git repository uses the proxy as an HTTP proxy and does not build this command.
Anyone who can create or update a repository or a repository credential template can set the proxy. That includes a project-scoped repository permission, `argocd repo add --proxy`, and a repository Secret. A credential template applies its proxy to every matching SSH repository that does not have its own credentials. Argo CD runs the command when it tests the repository connection and on later fetches. The process can read other Git, Helm, and OCI credentials stored for the repo-server.
### Patches
A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:
* v3.6.0-rc2 * v3.5.4 * v3.4.10 * v3.3.15
The fix stops passing the proxy host and port through a shell.
Argo CD 2.x and 3.0 through 3.2 are out of support and will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.
### Workarounds
There is no setting that keeps SSH repository proxies and removes the shell command.
* Do not grant repository create or update to untrusted users, including project-scoped repository access. See [RBAC resources](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/rbac/#rbac-model-structure) and [project-scoped repositories](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/#project-scoped-repositories-and-clusters). * Do not set a proxy on an SSH repository or on a credential template that matches SSH repositories. The proxy field is documented in [Configure repositories with proxy](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/declarative-setup/#configure-repositories-with-proxy). Credential templates are documented in [Credential templates](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/private-repositories/#credential-templates). The `--proxy` flag is documented in [`argocd repo add`](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/commands/argocd_repo_add/).
An HTTPS Git repository with an HTTP proxy does not use this command. Review existing repository and credential-template Secrets for unexpected `proxy` values.

item.title: [HIGH] zammad/zammad — Local privilege escalation to root in DEB/RPM packages (packager.io) (CVE-2026-102490)
item.description:
CVE-2026-102490 · CVSS 8.5 (CVSS:4.0/AV:L/AC:L/AT:N/PR:L/UI:N/VC:H/VI:H/VA:H/SC:N/SI:N/SA:N) · CWE-250, CWE-426, CWE-732
Affected: - other/Zammad <= 7.2.1 (patched: 7.2.2)
---
Zammad packages built with packager.io (DEB and RPM) could have allowed a local attacker who already had code execution as the unprivileged `zammad` service account to escalate to full `root` privileges on the host. Service processes began running as `root` and executed files that were owned and writable by the `zammad` account before dropping to that account, and the installation directory was writable by it. An attacker holding that foothold could have escalated within seconds, because the affected services were restarted automatically whenever they stopped; no administrator interaction was required. Only installations from the DEB and RPM packages were affected — installations from source or the official container images were not. All released packaged versions were affected.
Credit: The Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure Foundation (DIVD)

item.title: [MEDIUM] argoproj/argo-cd — An oversized OCI manifest can exhaust repo-server memory
item.description:
CVSS 6.5 (CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:N/A:H)
Affected: - go/github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3 >= 3.1.0, < 3.3.15 || >= 3.4.0, < 3.4.10 || >= 3.5.0, < 3.5.4 || = 3.6.0-rc1 (patched: 3.3.15, 3.4.10, 3.5.4, 3.6.0-rc2)
---
### Impact
Argo CD reads an OCI image manifest into memory with no size limit. A registry can return a manifest large enough to exhaust the repo-server. Kubernetes then kills the process, and manifest generation stops for every Application until the pod restarts. The same request can be sent again after the restart.
All versions from v3.1.0 onward are affected, including every currently supported release. v3.0.23 and earlier are not. The behavior was introduced in [18c4d9d568](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/commit/18c4d9d56869531f7ae017d610d4e79aaa5525c3) (2025-06-06, [#18646](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/pull/18646)), the change that added OCI as an application source, and was first released in v3.1.0.
Argo CD downloads the manifest when it renders an Application whose source is an OCI registry, and when it loads that source's metadata. Resolving a tag to a digest does not download the manifest. The `--oci-manifest-max-extracted-size` flag (default 1G) limits the unpacked image archive. It does not limit the manifest document. See [argocd-repo-server](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/server-commands/argocd-repo-server/).
Someone who can make Argo CD pull from a registry they control can trigger this. That includes creating an Application with an `oci://` source, which the `default` project's `sourceRepos: ['*']` allows. See [OCI](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/oci/) and [the default project](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/#the-default-project). A person who can push to a registry an Application already uses can do the same. This is the OCI counterpart of the Helm index limit in [GHSA-jhwx-mhww-rgc3](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/security/advisories/GHSA-jhwx-mhww-rgc3).
### Patches
A patch for this vulnerability has been released in the following Argo CD versions:
* v3.6.0-rc2 * v3.5.4 * v3.4.10 * v3.3.15
The fix rejects an OCI manifest larger than 4 MiB.
Argo CD 3.1 and 3.2 are affected and out of support. They will not receive a patch. Upgrade to a patched 3.3 or newer release.
### Workarounds
There is no setting that caps the OCI manifest document.
* Allow only registries you trust in the AppProject `sourceRepos` list. The `default` project allows every source until that list is changed. See [Projects](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user-guide/projects/). * Do not grant untrusted users permission to create Applications or repositories that point at other registries. See [RBAC resources](https://argo-cd.readthedocs.io/en/stable/operator-manual/rbac/#rbac-model-structure).
A user who can push to a registry already listed in `sourceRepos` can still publish an oversized manifest.
### Credits
The Argo CD team would like to thank @andrejtomci for responsibly disclosing this issue according to our [security reporting guidelines](https://github.com/argoproj/argo-cd/blob/master/SECURITY.md#reporting-a-vulnerability).
